title: The Ten Commandments (CCC 2052–2074)
hook: two tablets: love of God, love of neighbor; Catholics number them as Augustine did

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. Your line was the hinges. Today, ten words from a mountain, and a question of counting.

Ask a room full of people to list the Ten Commandments and something funny happens. Thou shalt not kill and thou shalt not steal come fast. Then it gets vague. Someone says be nice to your parents. Someone says no idols, someone else says that's not one of them, and a friendly argument starts about what number seven is. Both sides might be right. Christians and Jews have counted the same verses in different ways for a very long time. But before the counting, there's a mountain, a people just freed from slavery, and a voice.
screen: `KILL AND STEAL COME FAST.` → `WHAT NUMBER IS SEVEN?` → `A MOUNTAIN, AND A VOICE.`

segments.voice: It begins not with a rule but with a rescue. In the Douay-Rheims, God says: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." The commandments are given to people just set free, as the way to stay free. Decalogue is Greek for ten words; the Bible itself calls them the ten words, in Hebrew aseret ha-devarim. Moses comes down with two tablets of stone. The Church, following Augustine, puts three commandments on the first, about loving God: no other gods, honoring God's name, keeping the Lord's day holy. Seven go on the second, about loving neighbor: honor your parents, don't kill, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't covet your neighbor's wife, don't covet your neighbor's goods. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus sums up both tablets: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart," and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two tablets, one love. Now the counting. Catholics and Lutherans follow Augustine: no other gods and no images as one commandment, and coveting split into two. Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches count images as a separate second commandment, and coveting as one. Jewish tradition counts I am the Lord thy God as the first word. The verses are the same. Each tradition counts them its own way, and none of them leaves anything out.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH A RESCUE.` · `DECALOGUE: TEN WORDS.` · `THREE FOR GOD, SEVEN FOR NEIGHBOR.` · `SAME VERSES, COUNTED DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TWO TABLETS, ONE LOVE.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read Exodus 20, verses 1 to 17, slowly; all seventeen take about two minutes. If you can't, walk through the ten in your head, three for God, seven for neighbor, and stop at the one that speaks to your week, without grading yourself. If you pray, you can bring that one to God.
Decalogue. Greek for ten words: the Ten Commandments given at Sinai, which Jesus summed up as love of God and love of neighbor. Today's word.
Your line: two tablets, one love. The week walked from freedom and conscience, through sin, the Beatitudes and the virtues, to the ten words. Day three hundred fifteen, and a week complete.
